title: My Open Comment on Psychedelic Medicine to FDA
subtitle: I submitted this, I hope you submitted yours, and tune in on September 14th for the live comments.
body_html:
The FDA is having another live meeting in which open comments on psychedelic medicines will be heard. The last time something like this happened, it went poorly for MDMA-AT. But that was an AdComm about a specific trial program with…issues.

This is not that. It is FDA soliciting advice from the public on a variety of matters as it applies to all psychedelic medicines.

Below, I share my open comments…

Comment to Docket No. FDA-2026-N-7542

Considerations for Potential Future Therapeutic Use of Psychedelic Drugs; Public Hearing; Request for Comments

Submitted by: Owen Scott Muir, M.D., DFAACAP, FCTMSS Co-founder and Chief Medical Officer, Radial Health, Inc.; author, The Frontier Psychiatrists (thefrontierpsychiatrists.substack.com)

Topic addressed: Section III, Considerations for Access

Disclosure of financial relationships: I am an executive of Radial Health, Inc., a national clinic network delivering interventional psychiatric treatments including esketamine (Spravato) and transcranial magnetic stimulation, and of Neurolief, Inc. I hold financial interests in, or advise, companies in health technology and life sciences, including BrainsWay, Videra Health, iRxReminder, Purple Gaze, Psyrin, Outro Health, Brainify.ai, Acacia Clinics, AMPA Health, Definium, and Atai. I have direct financial interests in the delivery of the class of therapies discussed in this comment.

Summary

The constraint on patient access to FDA-approved psychedelic therapies is likely to be financial. The supply chain that made oral drugs accessible is essentially not relevant to the deployment of psychedelic medicines. It’s crucial the risk evaluation and mitigation strategies as part of FDA labels are designed with the reimbursement landscape in mind. The clinics that become the outpatient distribution centers become the “distribution channel” for these medicines, and as such, it needs to be economically viable for individual clinics and large clinic operators alike to dispense these medicines. I believe it’s in the best interest of patients to make it possible for all operators, not just those already at massive scale, to have access to these treatments. Please consider my comments in that context.

I write from seven years of direct clinical experience. One of my clinics was the first clinic in Brooklyn to dispense esketamine. Radial, the clinical services company that I co-founded, dispenses ketamine and provides neuromodulation, including SNT and Swift across 27 sites in rural and urban locations across 7 states.

Ketamine is the closest existing predicate for supervised and monitored administration of the model, so its reimbursement history is instructive. Contemplated for compounds like COMP360, MDMA, lysergide, ibogaine, and others. .

A. Evidence needs for coverage, benefit design, reimbursement, and payment models

The esketamine model demonstrated, by using existing current procedural terminology codes, reimbursement for consciousness altering therapeutics was scalable. It was possible to get a novel therapeutic to market through a Buy and Bill infrastructure, e.g. the clinics can purchase drugs and dispense it subsequently with some profit margin involved for the operator. The REMS program made this economically more viable because of the high risk being mitigated to the patient by definition (in that 99215 codes are allowed as standard with it’s higher reimbursement because the risk is contemplated in the code). The current consideration of REMS programs should make the duration as clear as the esketamine REMS did. It’s also worth noting that the current “psychedelic therapy” category III codes only allow for up to 6 hours of total monitoring, which may not be enough for the programs you’re considering for some of these compounds.

The REMS program will drive the reimbursement infrastructure. Physician time is a primary cost, but the total practice expense plus physician time that the REMS implies is crucial to consider when crafting the label along with the study sponsor. The current reimbursement infrastructure used by ketamine is a workaround that didn’t involve creating a robust new code set, which will almost certainly need to be the case to encompass all the psychedelic treatments that are coming. I would encourage working closely with your colleagues at CMS to make sure that the code sets and their adoption by Medicare are ready to lead the way along with the FDA approval and the risk evaluation of mitigation strategies as part of those approvals.

2. The billing architecture has a time limit at approximately two hours.

The Medically Unlikely Edit on 99417 is four units per day, which adds only 1 hour to the 40 min of a 99215 parent code (by time). Esketamine is still more time than that ceiling, but only by 20 minutes. Nearly every psychedelic in late-stage development (psilocybin, MDMA, LSD, ibogaine, methylone and more ) all will need complexity based billing and longer monitoring–thanks to the longer acting effects compared to ketamine and esketamine– more similar to surgical procedures than current psychiatric practice.

Absent working closely with CMS, and with the American Medical Association, there is no way to currently bill in outpatient psychiatric practice for a psych medicine procedure greater than six hours. This doesn’t mean your REMS should be limited to anything less than the safest interval, but it does mean that any monitoring for six hours needs to involve coordination with other agencies to ensure it can actually be delivered.

Another workaround would be for those agencies to adopt an oncology-style buy and bill coding around the J, S, and G codes that could be used to account for the dispensing and treatment with these compounds.

This planning cannot be an afterthought. It would be commercially and clinically disastrous for patients to have approved medicines that had no plausible means of reimbursement in the clinic itself, which is the current state of the world in any treatment lasting

3. Recommendation: payment pathways should be established concurrent with approval, not after. Medicare’s creation of bundled G codes for esketamine is an example of a correct template: a single payment encompassing drug acquisition, administration, and the full REMS-defined monitoring period, tiered by dose and session length. Waiting for post-approval rate negotiation, payer by payer and code by code, is itself an access barrier measured in years. Executive Order 14401 directs interagency coordination on access to these therapies; coordinated FDA–CMS sequencing of REMS finalization and payment-code creation is exactly the kind of coordination that would matter most. It would also be acceptable to use the current category III codes for therapy and a G/J Code to account for the “buy-and-bill” activity ONLY, that is likely to be necessary.

4. Recommendation: consider percentage-of-drug-price margin structures and complexity base billing for clinical services.

The experience in oncology of using average sale price (ASP) +6% demonstrates that tying clinician decision-making around the economics of a margin associated with the drug price creates a documented incentive towards more expensive treatments. That said, pairing the reimbursement for physician time to the complexity and risk of the REMS would be more in keeping with traditional “risk based” E+M coding that is the main state of current CPT coding methodology.

I believe that tying reimbursement to the psychedelic REMS program for the particular drug is a viable adjunctive to ASP +6%. The payment needs to compensate the complexity and expense of the service, which of course includes clinical and physician time, monitoring, facility infrastructure, which is well above the traditional practice expense associated with psychiatry, or even neurology, as well as the capital necessary to acquire what are likely to be expensive drugs. These rates need to take into account the fact that these drugs are likely to rise in price, and a drug price multiplier may need to be included in the calculation. This preserves the access that oncology achieved, with broad availability of new treatments without creating unintended incentive to prescribe preferentially more expensive drugs and ignoring the complexity of physician care in the prescribing of these novel compounds.

5. Evidence generation should include delivery-model economics, not only clinical endpoints.

Coverage decisions will require economic data on the cost utility of these compounds, which is very much in keeping with what has been proposed in the TCET program and similar to the log laid out in the not-yet-passed Breakthrough Treatments Act. I believe a version of the breakthrough treatments plan: creating mandatory Medicare payment within three months of approval of the drug, along with mandatory collection of pharmacoeconomic data, and review of reimbursement infrastructure after four years of deployment.

6. Preparation and coordination between providers and payors

Esketamine demonstrated that a lack of operational readiness and a lack of clear reimbursement pathways from payers means years of delay in getting already approved treatments to patients in need. It’s “ramp up time” to commercial viability took years, and that would undercut financial support for these new treatments in the minds of financial markets, thus limiting future innovation.

CMS can lead the way, partnering with FDA, to prepare a code set that would allow for dispensing of these medicines under Medicare rules that will be easier to follow for private payors.

The FDA and federal partners should convene certified sites, third-party payors, Study sponsors, and companies responsible for adjudicating prior authorization to understand what the workflow is likely to be so that it can be expedited.

The definitions around who can prescribe these treatments needs to take into account the fact that all those psychiatrists have the greatest expertise in the management of psychiatric conditions, it may be teams of Psychiatrist and other health professionals, including other physician, practice types that may be involved in the dispensing of these medications.

What is acceptable according to Medicare is likely to be followed by other payors, and thus “getting that right” when it comes to the mandatory standards around physician and clinician licensed type, experience, additional training, certification, and the light can be built into the REMS models and the reimbursement infrastructure.

C. Implementation: workforce, space, scheduling, storage, security, and clinic capacity

A second out capable clinic will require dedicated treatment, per-patient rooms occupied for most of our working dayt, with monitoring personnel, secure, drug storage, compliant with rims and DEA requirements, audiovisual, and IT infrastructure for audit monitoring will also be required.

These are both capital and operating expenses that will be paid by whoever owns the delivery site. Reimbursement needs to take these costs into account. If reimbursement does not count for them, the only entities able to observe the losses will be large, vertically, integrated organizations, the same organizations that have come under significant criticism recently.

Given set and setting are likely to be crucial factors of the deployment of these treatments, I think it’s important to have a collaborative approach around allocating value to appropriate set and setting, as well as as carefully monitoring outcomes.

We want reimbursement models that support payers working with physician owned professional, corporations, and hospitals alike. Independently owned, and physician lead practices are a bulwark against further inadvisable market consolidation, which these medications, rolled out without concern for the underlying economics, could make more common place.

Payment model should be tested against a simple question: can an independent practice deliver these treatments at the rates set for by payers without losing money? If the answer is no, access will narrow, regardless of how many products the FDA approves.

Our published experience with accelerated neuromodulation protocols demonstrates that reducing required visits materially improves treatment initiation and completion without sacrificing outcomes (Hanlon et al., 2026; Roth et al., 2023). The same logic applies to psychedelic delivery: protocol designs, monitoring technologies, and staffing models that increase patients treated per room per week are access interventions, and evidence supporting them should be treated as valuable contributions to the evidence base.

D. Telehealth screening, follow-up, and care coordination

Remote and technology-assisted assessment can extend scarce specialist capacity across the phases of care surrounding the monitored session itself. Two lines of my published work are directly relevant as predicates:

First, validated video-based AI assessment. Our peer-reviewed studies demonstrate that smartphone-recorded, self-administered video assessments scored by machine learning can detect a psychiatric adverse effect (tardive dyskinesia) with reliability exceeding calibrated human raters, including in remote settings (Sterns et al., 2025; Trosch et al., 2026). This supports the feasibility of standardized, scalable remote screening and longitudinal safety follow-up for psychedelic therapies — precisely the data-collection substrate contemplated in Section III of this notice.

Second, passive physiological monitoring during monitored administration. Our proof-of-concept study of a continuous passive monitoring system during 129 Spravato sessions demonstrated high data quality and usability for both patients and providers (Solomon et al., 2023). Technology-assisted monitoring can reduce per-session staffing burden while improving the auditability of REMS compliance — a rare intervention that serves safety and access simultaneously.

Telehealth should therefore be presumptively appropriate for screening, preparation, and follow-up phases, with in-person requirements reserved for the administration and monitoring phase where they belong. Blanket in-person requirements across all phases of care would function as a geographic access restriction without a corresponding safety benefit.

Conclusion

For the first time in psychiatry, a class of medicines cannot reach patients without clinicians and clinical infrastructure in the loop. That is an opportunity to build a delivery and payment system better aligned with patient outcomes than the rebate-driven pharmacy-benefit model it will not use anyway. The Agency and its federal partners should treat reimbursement architecture, session-length billing ceilings, and clinic-level economics as core access questions — because they are the questions that will determine whether approved psychedelic therapies reach the patients the clinical trials were run for.

Respectfully submitted,

Owen Scott Muir, M.D., DFAACAP, FCTMSS

References

  • Hanlon CA, Roth Y, Bermudes RA, ... MacMillan C, Muir O, ... Tendler A. Accelerated TMS with the H1-coil for depression: a multisite, randomized non-inferiority trial. Brain Stimulation. 2026;19(2):103050. doi:10.1016/j.brs.2026.103050

  • Roth Y, Hanlon CA, Pell G, Zibman S, Harmelech T, Muir OS, MacMillan C, et al. Real world efficacy and safety of various accelerated deep TMS protocols for major depression. Psychiatry Research. 2023. PMID: 37738684

  • Sterns AA, Hughes JW, Grimm B, Larsen L, Ma F, Ranjan R, ... Muir OS. Detecting tardive dyskinesia using video-based artificial intelligence. Journal of Clinical Psychiatry. 2025;86(3):25m15792. doi:10.4088/JCP.25m15792

  • Trosch R, Sterns A, Grimm B, Larsen L, Talbot B, Ma F, Ranjan R, MacMillan C, Hughes J, Friedman J, Muir O. Cross-dataset evaluation of an automated video-based model for detecting tardive dyskinesia using the Clinician’s Tardive Inventory: validation study. 2026. PMID: 42133936

  • Solomon N, Hajduk M, Majernik M, ... Muir O, ... Karlin D, Barrow B. Evaluating passive physiological data collection during Spravato treatment. 2023. PMCID: PMC10716422

  • Feyder, M. T., Stimpson, K. H., Geoly, A. D., Ford, T. J., Maron-Katz, A., Lutkenhoff, E., ... & Bentzley, B. S. (2026). Real-world evidence of SAINT® effectiveness in a heterogenous clinical population with psychiatric and medical comorbidities: A multicenter, open-label, community-based study. Journal of Mood & Anxiety Disorders, 14, 100184.

Thanks for following along. I can’t emphasize enough how much open comments matter in our crucial regulatory process—your voice matters!

A special thanks to Kenneth Shinozuka, Ph.D. for his collaboration on the editing of the comments.
